Common questions for Home. Tap a topic to expand the answer.
Tap the clear card. It is the free Control panel. This walkthrough uses Default and Classic Simple. No Pro and no camera.
Tap the clear cable icon. It opens connection settings with the free starter link already selected: Default and Classic Simple.

The clear section is the free setup: user type Default, board DevKit, and Bluetooth Classic + Simple (text lines). It matches TeleCon_Classic_Simple, which advertises ESP32-TC-RC-BT-Simple. Leave Advanced unused. Then tap the clear matching-firmware link and save or share that ZIP. The tutorial continues when the code is downloaded.
Choose Save to Downloads or Share. The tutorial continues when the code is saved or shared.

Upload TeleCon_Classic_Simple to the ESP32 in Arduino IDE (board ESP32 Dev Module). Open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and press RESET on the board. The capture above is what you should see: the ready banner and the name ESP32-TC-RC-BT-Simple. Press Continue only when that Serial Monitor is open and ready to receive the Bluetooth connection.
Arduino IDE Serial Monitor showing the TeleCon Classic Simple ready banner
Tap the clear Bluetooth icon. It opens the device list for this module.

The clear areas are refresh and the device lists. Tap refresh if the scan has stopped. Under Scanned Devices, tap ESP32-TC-RC-BT-Simple. If Android asks for a PIN, enter 1234. The tutorial continues when the status shows Connected.
Drag the clear left stick. The tutorial continues when it moves. Motion is a live session only after Connected. Official firmware echoes the gauges on the bench.

Double-tap a clear stick to open its settings. Spring returns it when you let go. Hold keeps the last position. You can limit that to vertical or horizontal, and choose the range shape. Each stick is configured on its own. The tutorial continues when that menu opens.

The clear area is the left side. The knob sends 0–255. Double-tap it to pick its telemetry channel. Three switches sit beside each stick. Double-tap a numeric panel or round gauge to set its label, channel, and, for panels, color and on/off. Tap Next when you want to continue.

The clear column switches the center view. Swipe it up or down to try another view. Plots is free and shows live traces. Stick draws the stick path. Camera shows an ESP32-CAM picture. Radar draws a sweep from telemetry. Stick, Camera, and Radar stay locked until you unlock them with coins or Pro. Plots does not. Tap Done when you want to finish.
ESP32 does not appear when scanning

Power on the ESP32 and press RESET. In Arduino IDE, open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and confirm the firmware ready banner. Grant Nearby devices if Android asks. From a module, open Bluetooth, tap refresh to scan, move closer, and stop scanning when your board appears under Scanned Devices.

Open a module from Home, then use its Bluetooth button to scan and connect. If the board was paired before, try Paired Devices. If it still fails, forget the device in Android Bluetooth settings, scan again, and pair from Scanned Devices. Match Classic/BLE and Simple/Binary to your sketch.

Home shows the last session status. Open a module from Home, then connect Bluetooth there. Only one phone should control the ESP32 at a time — close other apps using the link. When connected, Home updates to Connected and highlights your recent module.
Module controls or telemetry do nothing

Connect Bluetooth inside the module first. Confirm matching firmware and protocol in module settings (Classic Simple, Classic Binary, BLE Binary, or SoftAP where supported). Stay on the live screen while testing. Reflash the matching sketch from Codes and Documents if the Serial Monitor never shows a ready banner.
First-time setup — where do I start?

On Home, open Control panel (free) or RC Vehicle. Use the docs icon for the ESP32 ZIP and guides. Upload the sketch in Arduino IDE, connect Bluetooth from the module toolbar, and use module settings to match the protocol. Your last module stays highlighted on Home.
How do I open modules from Home?

Tap the front module card on Home to open it. Swipe the stack horizontally to bring another module to the front; with more than two modules you can swipe both ways. Expand the title for details, docs, or coin unlock. About this App is at the bottom of Home. When more modules ship, Browse Catalog appears on Home for the full list.
How do Pro modules and the sparkle work?

PRO modules need a subscription, coins, or an unlock grant. Tap Go Pro at the bottom of Home to open subscription options, or unlock a locked card with coins. The sparkle is an occasional explorer gift: watch an ad for a short Pro trial. When a Pro module is enabled it keeps the PRO badge and shows a pulsing green border; the sparkle hides until the gift is available again.

Match the blue numbered badges on the Home screen image (1–6) to the items below.

1. Quick Start (bottom): reconnects to the last saved Bluetooth device, or sends you to scan for a new device.

2. Catalog: opens the module catalog (Control panel, Smart home, and more). Tap a module to open it.

4. Codes and Documents: opens PDF guides and lets you share or save the ESP32_BT_Controller-main.zip code file.

5. Tutorial: opens this step-by-step app guide.

This video shows how to prepare the ESP32 in Arduino IDE:

- Open ESP32_BT_Controller.ino in Arduino IDE (download the ZIP from the app in step 2 if you do not have the sketch yet).

- Select the correct ESP32 board under Tools > Board.

- Select the serial port connected to your ESP32 under Tools > Port.

- Upload the sketch to the ESP32.

- Open Tools > Serial Monitor and set the baud rate to 115200.

- Press the ESP32 RESET button.

- Confirm the monitor prints: ESP32 Bluetooth Receiver Ready.

- When you see that message, the ESP32 is waiting for a Bluetooth connection from the app (step 4).

This video shows how to get the project files from the app:

- Open Codes and Documents on the Home screen and tap the ESP32 BT Controller ZIP item.

- Choose Share or send to email or messaging, or Save to Downloads to keep a copy on the phone.

- Open the ZIP where you saved it or from the app you shared to.

- Extract the archive if needed and locate ESP32_BT_Controller.ino.

- Transfer the folder to your computer if you uploaded from the phone, then continue with step 3 in Arduino IDE.
Connect to the ESP32 with Bluetooth

This GIF shows how to connect the app to the ESP32-BT device:

- From the Home screen, tap the Bluetooth button.

- On the Bluetooth screen, tap the refresh icon in the top app bar to start scanning.

- When ESP32-BT appears, tap the X icon to stop scanning.

- Check the Scanned Devices list and find ESP32-BT.

- If this is the first connection, tap ESP32-BT from Scanned Devices to pair and connect.

- If the ESP32 was already paired before, tap ESP32-BT from Paired Devices to connect faster.

- After the connection succeeds, the app returns to the Home screen.

- Confirm that the Bluetooth button now shows the Connected status.

This video shows how to review and apply the controller settings:

- From the Home screen (Bluetooth Connected), tap Catalog.

- Open Control panel, then tap the settings icon in the top bar to open Control panel settings.

- On RC Controller Settings, review Joystick Settings and choose the behavior for the left and right sticks.

- Review Initial Switch Positions and set the starting state for switches S1 to S6.

- Review Initial Knob Values and set the starting value for the left and right knobs.

- Return to the Home screen after the configuration is saved.

- Tap Catalog again, then tap Control panel to open the controller.

- Confirm that joystick behavior, switch states, and knob values are applied correctly on the RC screen.

The RC Control screen runs in landscape. The numbers on the image match this list:

1. Header indicators — Left: analog gauge with integer value and title from ESP32 telemetry. Right: battery-style level and title from telemetry. Both update when the firmware sends new indicator data.

2. Seven-segment displays — Left and right numeric panels (for example RPM). Titles, on/off, and green/red color are set in Panel settings; firmware sends the numeric values.

3. Status LEDs — Four LEDs on each side (eight total). Left uses the lower four bits of the LED byte; right uses the upper four. Each LED lights when its bit is set in incoming telemetry.

4. Joysticks — Left and right 3D sticks. Drag to send X and Y in the control packet. Return behavior (spring, hold, etc.) is set per side under Joystick Settings in RC Controller Settings.

5. Switches (S1–S6) — Three toggles on the left (S1–S3) and three on the right (S4–S6). Each maps to a bit in the switch byte; initial on/off states are configured in settings.

6. Rotary knobs — Left and right knobs. Turn to set a 0–100% style auxiliary value sent continuously to the ESP32.

7. Action buttons — Four momentary buttons (upper and lower on each side). Press to send one-shot event packets: CENTER_TOP_LEFT, CENTER_BOTTOM_LEFT, CENTER_TOP_RIGHT, and CENTER_BOTTOM_RIGHT.

8. Center telemetry plot — Live graph area fed by Bluetooth plot series from the ESP32.

While this screen is open, control packets are sent continuously. Connect over Bluetooth before opening RC Control so telemetry and inputs stay in sync with the ESP32.

This video tests every RC screen component from step 6 while the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor runs at 115200 baud next to the app.

Bench debug is the same for Classic Simple, Classic Binary, and BLE Binary (match Connection type in RC Settings to your sketch):

- Firmware default is simulate mode: sticks/knobs/switches on the phone are echoed into panel, indicator, LED, and plot telemetry (no extra wiring).

- Set `TELECON_DEBUG` / `TELECON_SERIAL_INJECT` to 1 (or Classic Binary equivalent) and open Serial Monitor at 115200.

- Connect over Bluetooth, open RC Control, complete handshake (`RC:ACK`).

What the video should show (same order as step 6):

1. Header indicators — Move left/right knobs; analog and battery gauges follow. Serial may log TX telemetry.

2. Seven-segment displays — Move left/right sticks; panel numbers follow stick X (or your firmware mapping).

3. Status LEDs — Toggle switches; LED bits follow the switch byte.

4. Joysticks — Move left then right sticks; Serial shows RX control (text `RC:CTRL` or binary `AA 55`).

5. Switches (S1–S6) — Toggle each switch; confirm RX switch bits and LED feedback.

6. Rotary knobs — Turn both knobs; confirm RX knob values and gauge feedback.

7. Action buttons — Press each side button; Serial shows `RC:BTN` or `BB 66` event.

8. Center plot — Move sticks/knobs; four plot traces update. Labels come from RC Settings → Plot labels.

Optional: type a protocol line in Serial Monitor (`TELECON_SERIAL_INJECT`) to inject telemetry toward the phone (same idea on Classic and BLE).

When finished, center sticks and return controls to a safe default before driving real hardware (`TELECON_USE_HW_IO 1`).

This video shows how to drive the left and right seven-segment displays on the RC screen (step 6, item 2).

Bench setup (same for Classic Simple, Classic Binary, and BLE Binary):

- Flash the matching Control Panel sketch with simulate / echo mode (`TELECON_USE_HW_IO 0` on BLE; Classic Simple auto-echo; Classic Binary after the unified debug update).

- In RC Settings, select the connection mode that matches the sketch, then connect and open RC Control.

- Open Serial Monitor at 115200 if you want TX/RX logs.

What the video should show:

- Move the left stick — left panel value tracks the mapping (typically stick X → 0–9999).

- Move the right stick — right panel updates the same way.

- Optional Serial inject (when `TELECON_SERIAL_INJECT` is 1):
 Classic Simple: `RC:DATA,left,100,right,200,analog,42,batt,88,led,0F`
 Classic/BLE Binary: use firmware inject helpers or stick echo (binary `CC 11` is sent automatically).

If panels do not update, verify handshake ACK, connection mode matches the sketch, and RC Control is open.
Test analog, battery, and LED telemetry

This video shows how to test the left analog indicator, right battery indicator, and status LEDs on the RC screen (step 6, items 1 and 3).

Bench setup (same for Classic Simple, Classic Binary, and BLE Binary):

- Use simulate / echo firmware (sticks and knobs feed gauges; switch byte feeds LEDs).

- Match Connection type in RC Settings to the sketch, connect, open RC Control.

What the video should show:

- Turn the left knob — left analog gauge follows (0–255 mapping).

- Turn the right knob — battery indicator follows.

- Toggle switches — status LEDs follow the switch bitfield.

- Optional Serial inject of `RC:DATA,...,analog,75,batt,90,led,0F` on Classic Simple, or rely on binary `CC 22` echo on Classic/BLE Binary.

If nothing updates, verify Bluetooth handshake, mode match, and that simulate mode is enabled (not HW-only with no sensors).

This video shows how plot channel labels are set in the app and how four live plot channels drive the center graph on the RC screen (step 6, item 8).

Part 1 — Plot labels in RC Controller Settings:

- Open RC Controller Settings.

- Set Plot 1–4 (for example "Volts", "Amps", "RPMs", "Temp"). Firmware no longer sends `RC:PLOTCFG` / `CC 44` names.

Part 2 — Bench plot values (same for Classic Simple, Classic Binary, and BLE Binary):

- Use simulate / echo firmware: plot channels map from knobs/sticks (typically lk, lx, rk, ry → v0…v3 / four `CC 33` bytes).

- Match Connection type to the sketch, connect, open RC Control so the dual-pane graph is visible.

- Move knobs and sticks — all four traces should update.

- Optional Serial inject on Classic Simple: `RC:PLOT,v0,120,v1,80,v2,200,v3,40`

If labels are wrong, edit Plot labels in settings. If the graph stays flat, verify handshake, mode match, and simulate/echo mode.
ESP32 sends 0–255. Calibrated value = offset + (byte / 255) × span. Default offset 0 and span 255 show the raw byte.

ESP32 sends numbered analog samples CH1–CH8 (v0–v7 on RC:PLOT / CC 33), plus analog, battery, panels, and LED bits on RC:DATA. This map only chooses which Control Panel widget shows each signal. Defaults match the stock layout. Four-sample firmware still works; extra channels stay at 0 until the sketch sends them.
